newsitem.title: USA: UPS, Teamsters meeting with federal negotiator.
newsitem.headline: UPS, Teamsters meeting with federal negotiator.

text.p: United Parcel Service and the Teamsters union met for last-ditch talks Thursday night with a federal negotiator, who said that at this late date every step to avoid a strike is "like climbing a mountain."
The two sides met only hours ahead of a midnight deadline for a strike that threatened to cripple the largest package carrier in the United States.

The adversaries got together briefly at the Washington Court Hotel, then left to settle down to serious talks at the National Mediation and Conciliation Service, said Brian Flores, national representative for the service.

"Time is getting short, there's only a few hours left," John Calhoun Wells, head of the mediation service, said at the hotel. "Both sides have agreed to my request to meet face to face. At this late stage, every step is like climbing a mountain."
Teamsters President Ron Carey said he was determined to try to reach agreement: "We're here to negotiate a contract, not a strike."
The two sides are negotiating a new five-year contract to replace the existing one, which expires at midnight.
If the approximately 200,000 Teamsters strike UPS, more than 12 million packages destined for roughly 1.5 million U.S. customers a day will be stranded, along with others overseas.
The key issues in the negotiations are creation of more full-time jobs, an end to subcontracting, safety and health issues, and pension issues, the union said.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said a senior adviser, Bruce Lindsey, had met with officials from both sides earlier Thursday, but an administration official said President BillClinton was not considering intervening.
Clinton intervened under the Railway Labour Act to end an American Airlines strike minutes after it began earlier this year.

But, to halt a UPS walkout, Clinton would have to use the cumbersome and time-consuming Taft-Hartley law, which has not been used since the 1950s, to order a mediation board to settle the dispute, the administration official said.
The company said earlier it had made its "last, best and final offer" Wednesday evening. The union rejected that offer.
If the strike takes place, Congress might be inclined to reconsider labour laws governing UPS, an analyst said.
The strike would idle approximately 200,000 Teamsters, two- thirds of the company's work force. The two sides even disagreed on that number: The union said 185,000 and the company 214,000.

A stumbling block in negotiations is the fate of part-timers at UPS, who make up more than half the union membership at the firm. The company has offered to convert roughly one in 10 of the part-time employees -- 10,000 of them -- to full-time work over the five-year contract. The union says that is not enough.
The company also wants to break up the Teamsters pension fund, substituting a joint company-union fund that includes only UPS employees.
"We believe UPS dollars should directly benefit UPS employees, not support the Teamsters' pension funds," said company spokesman Ken Sternad.
The company says that would improve pension benefits and might help it financially, as well.
"We anticipate in the long run there could be savings to UPS," Sternad said. A union spokesman declined to comment on the pension issue.
"We are not going to negotiate this in the media," said Rand Wilson.
But a union negotiator, who asked not to be identified, said if the company took over the pension plan, employees would be unable to switch firms and preserve their pensions.
The contract would increase top pay for full-time workers from $19.95 an hour to $21.45 by 2001 -- which the company says would be the highest in the industry.
The lowest paid part-time employees, who now earn $8 an hour, would get $11 an hour by 2001.
The union also objects to the use of subcontractors instead of union help.
If the strike does take place, the company's roughly 2,000 pilots -- who operate its 200 aircraft -- pledged to honour the picket line and not fly.

The company is the largest package carrier in the country, with 1996 revenues of $22.4 billion. It handles 3.15 billion parcels and documents shipped annually to more than 200 countries from 1,700 hubs and centres.
